chunks: Some of our companions, raising it (the chain), from Mufaddal ibn Umar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

O Mufaddal! He will not succeed who has no intellect, and he has no intellect who does not know. Soon he who understands will be distinguished, and he who is clement will be victorious. Knowledge is a shield, truthfulness is honour, ignorance is disgrace, understanding is glory, generosity is success, and good morals are a cause of affection.

The knowledgeable one of his time will not be assailed by confusions. Prudence is to expect the worst of conjectures. Between a person and wisdom, a scholar is a blessing; and the ignorant is wretched between the two. God is the protector of the one who truly knows Him, and the enemy of the one who pretends to know Him. The wise one is forgiving and the ignorant one is treacherous.
If you wish to be honoured, be gentle; and if you wish to be humiliated, be harsh. He whose origin is noble has a soft heart, and he whose nature is harsh has a hard liver.

He who is excessive will be entangled, and he who fears the consequences will refrain from plunging recklessly into what he does not know. He who rushes into a matter without knowledge will mutilate his own nose (pride). He who does not know will not understand, he who does not understand will not be safe, he who is not safe will not be honoured, he who is not honoured will be devoured, he who is devoured is most blameworthy, and he who is such is more deserving of regret.

key_terms.الحزم: Prudence, resolved caution; the Imam defines it as 'bad suspicion of conjecture' meaning not trusting one's unverified assumptions
key_terms.اللوابس: Confusions, ambiguities, doubtful matters that assail the ill-informed
key_terms.تكلفه: Pretending or feigning knowledge/closeness to God — contrasted with true recognition (معرفة)
key_terms.جدع أنف نفسه: Cutting off one's own nose — Arabic idiom for self-disgrace through recklessness
key_terms.جنة: Shield/protection — knowledge is compared to armour that defends against confusion and misguidance
key_terms.يعقل: Has intellect/reason ('aql) — in Shia thought, 'aql is not merely cognitive ability but a divinely-granted moral faculty

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Sadiq say about the relationship between knowledge, intellect, and success?
ai.summary: In this extended discourse addressed personally to Mufaddal ibn Umar — one of Imam al-Sadiq's closest companions, for whom a famous treatise on theodicy (Tawhid al-Mufaddal) was also composed — Imam al-Sadiq (AS) presents a systematic philosophy of knowledge, intellect, and character. The hadith employs a memorable parallel structure of aphorisms, contrasting knowledge with ignorance, reason with folly, gentleness with harshness. The culminating chain ('he who does not know → does not understand → is not safe → not honoured → is devoured → is blameworthy → deserves regret') was understood by early Muslim scholars as outlining the cascading social and spiritual consequences of ignorance.
word_analysis: raised it (attributed it up the chain)

en.hubeali:
One of our companions, raising it from Mufazzal Bin Umar, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said: ‘O Mufazzal!

He will not succeed, the one who has no intellect, nor would he have intellect, the one who does not know. Soon, the one who understands would be excellent, and the one who forbears would be victorious; and the knowledge is a shield, and the truthfulness is an honour, and the ignorance is a disgrace, and the understanding is a glory, and the benevolence is a success, and good morals are a cause for the cordiality.

And the knowledgeable one of his time would not be assaulted upon by the confusion. The strictness is an evil deed of the conjectures, and between the person and the wisdom a knowledgeable one is a Bounty, and the ignorant is a wretched between the two. And Allah<sup>azwj</sup> is a friend of the one who recognises Him<sup>azwj</sup> and an enemy of the one who pretends (to know Him<sup>azwj</sup>); and the intellectual is forgiving and the ignorant one is a fault-finder.

If you desire to be honoured, so be lenient, and if you desire to be abased (rejected), so be harsh. 
And the one whose origin is honourable, his heart would be soft, and the one whose ingredient is harshness, his liver would be thick; and the one who is excessive would get involved, and the one who fears the consequences would be steadfast from making incursions in that which he does not know.

And the one rushes into a matter without knowledge would mutilate the nose (pride) of his own self; and the one who does not know would not understand, and the one who does not understand would not submit, and the one who does not submit would not be honoured, and the one who is not honoured would be devoured, and the one who is devoured would be reproached, and the one who was like that, would be more likely to regret’.
